```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 10,
  fig.height = 5,
  out.width = "100%"
)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Problem 1: New York weather

I use the NOAA data from the course package rather than keeping a local copy. Each row is one station on one date; stations do not all report the same measurements or cover the same years.

```{r weather-import}
data("ny_noaa")

weather_missing <- ny_noaa |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing") |>
  mutate(percent_missing = 100 * missing / nrow(ny_noaa))

weather_missing |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Variable", "Missing observations", "Missing (%)")
  )
```

There are **`r format(nrow(ny_noaa), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables**, covering `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` New York stations from `r min(ny_noaa$date)` through `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. The variables are station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and daily maximum and minimum temperature. Temperature is stored as character text in the original data. Missingness is substantial: roughly 44% of both temperature variables are missing, compared with about 6% of precipitation, 15% of snowfall, and 23% of snow depth. These are missing measurements, not days with zero rain or snow. Comparisons below therefore describe the available records rather than a balanced set of stations.

### Cleaning and snowfall values

The [course data description](https://p8105.com/dataset_noaa.html) gives temperature in tenths of degrees Celsius and precipitation in tenths of millimeters. I convert those to degrees Celsius and millimeters. Snowfall and snow depth are already in millimeters. I also separate the date into year, month, and day. One snowfall value is negative (-13 mm); since snowfall cannot be negative, I replace that value with missing rather than turning it into zero.

```{r weather-clean}
weather <- ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    snow = if_else(snow < 0, NA_integer_, snow)
  )

snow_counts <- weather |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 6)

snow_counts |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Snowfall (mm)", "Station-days"))
```

Zero is by far the most common recorded snowfall: `r format(snow_counts$n[1], big.mark = ",")` station-days, or `r round(100 * mean(weather$snow == 0, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`% of nonmissing snowfall observations. That makes sense because snowfall is seasonal and many winter days also have no snow. The next common amounts, 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm, are close to 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches. This heaping is consistent with measurements recorded in inches and then converted and rounded to millimeters, rather than equally likely snowfall at every millimeter.

### January and July temperatures

I calculate the average daily maximum temperature within each station, year, and month. A station-month with no temperature observations has no mean to plot. I keep partly observed months and count their observed days so that an unusual mean can be checked against its coverage.

```{r weather-monthly}
station_month <- weather |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    observed_days = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(observed_days > 0) |>
  mutate(month = factor(month, levels = c(1, 7), labels = c("January", "July")))

station_month |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.18, linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey45") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 0.6, color = "#25658A") +
  facet_grid(~ month) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1985, 2010, 5)) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station",
    subtitle = "Each point is a station-month; lines connect the same station across years",
    x = "Year", y = "Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)"
  )
```

The seasonal difference is clear on the common temperature scale: July station means cluster around the upper 20s, while January means are near freezing. Many stations rise and fall together across years, suggesting shared warm or cold seasons. January varies more from year to year than July. Differences among stations also persist, but these data alone do not identify how much is due to geography, elevation, or reporting differences. Changing station coverage makes this a poor basis for a simple statewide warming claim.

The low July point in 1988 stands out. I check it directly, along with the coldest January station-month:

```{r weather-outliers}
station_month |>
  filter(
    (id == "USC00308962" & year == 1988 & month == "July") |
      (id == "USC00301723" & year == 1982 & month == "January")
  ) |>
  select(id, year, month, observed_days, mean_tmax) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Station", "Year", "Month", "Observed days", "Mean maximum (°C)")
  )
```

The July 1988 mean is only about 14°C at station USC00308962, even though all 31 days are observed; it is not explained by just one recorded day. The January 1982 mean of about -13.4°C at USC00301723 is also based on 31 days. These deserve investigation, but an outlying value alone does not establish an error. I retain them here. Some other station-months are based on very few days, so their averages need extra caution.

### Temperature relationship and snowfall distributions

A scatterplot would place more than a million points on top of each other. I use two-dimensional bins instead, with a logarithmic count scale so that dense regions and sparse observations are both visible. The second panel includes exactly the requested snowfall range, greater than 0 and less than 100 mm.

```{r weather-distributions, fig.height=8, fig.width=11}
temperature_plot <- weather |>
  drop_na(tmin, tmax) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 65) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey45") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "Station-days") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily maximum vs. minimum",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)", y = "Maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

snow_plot <- weather |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = factor(year))) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#B8D5E5", outlier.alpha = 0.2, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall on days with 0 < snow < 100 mm",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)", y = "Year"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10))

temperature_plot + snow_plot
```

Daily minimum and maximum temperatures have a strong positive relationship. Most observations lie above the dashed equality line, as expected. There are also sparse, questionable observations, including some below the line where the recorded minimum exceeds the maximum. The source has `r sum(weather$tmin > weather$tmax, na.rm = TRUE)` such pairs. I show them rather than silently removing them; the supplied data lack quality flags to resolve them. The most extreme temperatures should not be treated as reliable weather records without further checking.

For the selected positive snowfall amounts, the distributions are fairly similar across years: their medians are around 25 mm, with much of the data between roughly 13 and 51 mm. The repeated amounts also show up in these boxplots. This panel says how much snow was recorded **on selected snowy days**; it does not compare how often snow occurred or the total annual snowfall, since zero snowfall and values of 100 mm or more are excluded.

## Problem 2: NHANES activity

### Organizing the data

The demographic file begins with four lines of coding notes. I skip those lines, retain all five demographic variables, and use the file's definitions to label sex and education. Education is ordered from less than high school to more than high school. Age and BMI remain numeric, while the participant identifier is character.

```{r nhanes-import}
nhanes_covar_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 4,
  col_types = cols(SEQN = col_character(), .default = col_double())
) |>
  rename(seqn = SEQN, bmi = BMI)

nhanes_covar <- nhanes_covar_raw |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

nhanes_accel <- read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_accel.csv",
  col_types = cols(SEQN = col_character(), .default = col_double())
) |>
  rename(seqn = SEQN)

nhanes <- nhanes_covar |>
  left_join(nhanes_accel, by = "seqn") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(minute),
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )
```

Of the original `r nrow(nhanes_covar_raw)` participants, `r sum(nhanes_covar_raw$age < 21)` are younger than 21. Among the remaining adults, `r sum(nhanes_covar_raw$age >= 21) - nrow(nhanes_covar)` have missing demographic data, leaving **`r nrow(nhanes_covar)` participants**. I exclude missing BMI as well as missing sex, age, or education. Both input files have one row per participant and matching IDs, and there are no missing accelerometer values. The final long table has `r format(nrow(nhanes), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(nhanes)` columns: one row per participant-minute. It preserves the original demographic fields and every minute's activity value. Minute 1 begins at midnight, so it maps to hour 0 rather than 1/60.

### Education, sex, and age

I count people in the demographic table, where each participant appears once. Counting the long table would inflate every group by 1,440.

```{r nhanes-demographic-table}
education_counts <- nhanes_covar |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = Men + Women)

education_counts |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Education", "Men", "Women", "Total"))
```

The largest group has more than a high school education (115 people), about half the retained sample. Men and women have similar counts in that group and in the less-than-high-school group. The high-school-equivalent group has more men than women (35 versus 23), so its sex-specific patterns are based on unequal sample sizes.

```{r nhanes-age, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
sex_colors <- c("Men" = "#25658A", "Women" = "#C76824")

nhanes_covar |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, color = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.45, outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 8105),
    alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5
  ) +
  facet_grid(~ education, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 21)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = sex_colors) +
  labs(title = "Age distributions in the retained sample", x = NULL, y = "Age (years)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Participants with more than high school education tend to be younger: their median ages are 43.5 for men and 41 for women, versus 60 and 61 in the less-than-high-school group. In the high-school-equivalent group, the median age is higher for women (62 versus 53 for men), although the distributions overlap widely. All six groups span a broad range of adult ages. This age imbalance matters when interpreting activity differences across education or sex.

### Total activity and age

I sum the 1,440 minute-level MIMS values for each person to obtain total daily activity. No minutes are missing, so no imputation or missing-value removal is needed in this sum.

```{r nhanes-total, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.3}
nhanes_total <- nhanes |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims), .groups = "drop")

nhanes_total |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex, shape = sex, linetype = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.9, se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_grid(~ education, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 21)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = sex_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 80, 20)) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity and age",
    x = "Age (years)", y = "Total daily activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex", shape = "Sex", linetype = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Total activity generally decreases with age in each education group, with considerable variation among people of the same age. The decrease looks especially pronounced in the less-than-high-school group. Women tend to have higher totals than men in the more-than-high-school group, while the ordering is less consistent in the other panels. There are also a few unusually active individuals, which is a reason to read the smooth curves together with the points. These curves are descriptive and can be unstable near the ends of the age range; they do not adjust for BMI or other differences between participants.

### Activity over the day

To compare the time courses without drawing 228 overlapping individual traces, I first average activity at each minute within education and sex. Everyone has a complete day, so participants have equal weight in each minute's mean. The thin traces show these means; the heavier curves smooth the same means over roughly a few hours.

```{r nhanes-time-course, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.2}
activity_time <- nhanes |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute, hour) |>
  summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims), .groups = "drop")

activity_time |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex, linetype = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.12, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_grid(~ education, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 21)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = sex_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 24),
    breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24),
    labels = c("00:00", "06:00", "12:00", "18:00", "24:00")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean minute-level activity across the day",
    x = "Time of day", y = "Mean activity (MIMS per minute)",
    color = "Sex", linetype = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10))
```

All groups show low activity overnight, an increase in the morning, sustained daytime activity, and a decline in the evening. The largest sex separation appears in the more-than-high-school group, where women's daytime mean activity is generally higher. The high-school-equivalent group has more overlap, and differences in the less-than-high-school group change over the day rather than showing one sex consistently above the other. These are group averages, so they hide individual schedules. They also reflect the age mix shown above. Without survey weights or adjustment, I would describe these as patterns in the supplied sample rather than population estimates or causal effects of education.

## Problem 3: Citi Bike

### Importing and describing the rides

The four files have the same seven columns. I add year and month from their filenames before combining them, then order month, weekday, membership, and bike type for tables and plots. I keep rides with missing station names in the overall counts and duration summaries; a missing station name does not mean the ride did not happen.

```{r citibike-import}
citibike <- bind_rows(
  read_csv("data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
  read_csv("data/July 2020 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
  read_csv("data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
  read_csv("data/July 2024 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
) |>
  rename(weekday = weekdays) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekday = factor(
      weekday,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual, levels = c("casual", "member"), labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type, levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"), labels = c("Classic", "Electric")
    )
  )
```

The combined dataset contains **`r format(nrow(citibike), big.mark = ",")` rides and `r ncol(citibike)` variables**. Each ride has a unique ride ID, bike type, weekday, duration in minutes, starting and ending station names, membership status, year, and month. The data cover January and July in 2020 and 2024. There are `r sum(is.na(citibike$start_station_name))` missing starting station names and `r sum(is.na(citibike$end_station_name))` missing ending station names; the other fields are complete. Ride IDs are unique, and the observed durations range from about `r round(min(citibike$duration), 1)` to `r round(max(citibike$duration), 1)` minutes.

These files contain **1% samples of rides under four hours**, not every Citi Bike trip. The tables report counts in those samples. The duration distributions are also conditional on the source's duration restriction.

### Ride counts by month, year, and membership

```{r citibike-counts}
ride_counts <- citibike |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = Casual + Member)

ride_counts |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual rides", "Member rides", "Total rides"))
```

Members account for most rides in every month. July has more rides than January in both years, and the 2024 samples are larger than the corresponding 2020 samples. The July total rises from 21,048 to 47,156, about 2.24 times as many sampled rides. Casual rides make up a larger share in July than January: about 26.8% versus 7.9% in 2020, and 23.1% versus 11.2% in 2024. That suggests a stronger summer increase among casual riders. These comparisons describe the supplied months and should not be treated as a full-year trend.

### Most popular starting stations in July 2024

I rank named starting stations by the number of sampled rides originating there. Rides with an unknown starting station remain in the dataset but cannot identify a popular station.

```{r citibike-stations}
top_stations <- citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July", !is.na(start_station_name)) |>
  count(start_station_name, name = "rides", sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_stations |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Starting station", "Rides in July 2024 sample"))
```

Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers has the most starts (163), followed by University Pl & E 14 St (155). The remaining three stations are close together, at 146–152 rides. These are sample rankings; the small differences do not establish the same exact ranking in all July trips.

### Median duration across weekdays, months, and years

I take the median separately within each year, month, and weekday. The two panels share a duration scale, and the line colors and shapes identify the year.

```{r citibike-weekdays, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.2}
weekday_medians <- citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekday) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(year = factor(year))

weekday_medians |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = weekday, y = median_duration, group = year,
    color = year, shape = year, linetype = year
  )) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  facet_grid(~ month) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2020" = "#25658A", "2024" = "#C76824")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by weekday",
    x = "Day of the week", y = "Median duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year", shape = "Year", linetype = "Year"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

July rides have longer median durations than January rides on every weekday in both years. The 2020 medians are also higher than the 2024 medians for every corresponding month and weekday. The weekend increase is strongest in July 2020, when Saturday and Sunday medians are about 16.5 minutes, compared with roughly 13.4–14.2 on weekdays. July 2024 has a smaller weekend increase. January 2024 is fairly flat, including a Sunday median of about 7.4 minutes, so a blanket claim that weekend rides are always longer would miss that exception. Differences in riders and bike types could contribute to these patterns; the plot does not isolate the effect of the calendar itself.

### Duration distributions in 2024

The duration data have a long right tail. I use a logarithmic duration axis to show the main distributions and the longer rides together without dropping the tail. The violins show the distribution on that scale, and the small boxplots mark its median and middle half. Both panels use the same axis. Violin widths are standardized, so they should not be read as group sizes.

```{r citibike-distributions, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_violin(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    scale = "width", trim = TRUE, alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_grid(~ month) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Classic" = "#25658A", "Electric" = "#D99A43")) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(1, 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 240)) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration by membership and bike type in 2024",
    subtitle = "Logarithmic duration axis; violins include all rides in the 2024 samples",
    x = "Membership", y = "Duration (minutes, log scale)", fill = "Bike type"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Casual riders generally take longer rides than members, and the distributions are right-skewed in all groups. For casual riders, classic-bike medians exceed electric-bike medians in both months: about 12.7 versus 9.3 minutes in January, and 15.6 versus 12.9 in July. The pattern differs for members: the January medians are close (7.3 for classic and 7.6 for electric), while in July the electric-bike median is higher (9.2 versus 7.7). July shifts durations upward most clearly for casual riders and electric-bike members. There is no uniform pattern of electric bikes producing shorter rides. Riders choose their bikes and trips, so these are associations rather than evidence that bike type causes a change in duration.
